item.title: Supreme Court Blocks Trump Administration Plan to Screen Mail-In Ballots
item.description: The Trump administration had asked the justices to allow a new Postal Service plan to screen ballots just weeks before the midterm elections.
item.dc:creator: Abbie VanSickle
item.media:credit: Mike Kai Chen for The New York Times
item.media:description: A resident drops off her mail ballot in Livermore, Calif., last month.

item.title: Trump’s Effort to Assert Control Over Elections Continues Despite Supreme Court Loss
item.description: President Trump has launched a broad, governmentwide effort to take more control of state-run elections and sow doubt about the outcome.
item.dc:creator: Zolan Kanno-Youngs
item.media:credit: Rebecca Noble for The New York Times
item.media:description: Mail ballots await their mailing date in Phoenix in 2022.

item.title: Trump Administration Moves to Integrate A.I. Into Medical Care Despite Concerns
item.description: Federal projects are rolling out A.I. agents that offer therapy and prescribe medicine, raising concerns about safety and the influence of venture capital investors.
item.dc:creator: Christina Jewett
item.category: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
item.media:credit: Jeremie Souteyrat for The New York Times
item.media:description: A demonstration of a Limbic A.I. mental health app.

item.title: Trump Rejects Talk of A.I. Regulation and Calls Out Anthropic’s CEO
item.description: The president again rejected calls to try to regulate the industry, even as some of its leaders are speaking more openly about the risks of rapidly developing artificial intelligence.
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Swan and Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times
item.media:description: President Trump has spent much of his second term aligning himself with promoters of artificial intelligence who have been pushing the U.S. government to clear away obstacles to growth.

item.title: Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Gets Onstage Call From Trump, Who Dismissed A.I. Safety Concerns
item.description: Mr. Trump called Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, while Mr. Huang was onstage in Los Angeles and criticized calls to slow down and regulate A.I.
item.dc:creator: Kalley Huang, Mike Isaac and Karen Weise
item.media:credit: Manuel Orbegozo for The New York Times
item.media:description: Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, has been critical of worries over the safety of artificial intelligence.

item.title: As A.I. Fears Rise, Experts Suggest Focusing on the Humans in Charge
item.description: Warnings from industry leaders about doomsday scenarios ignore the power that people have to control how artificial intelligence is used, policy experts say. They are urging lawmakers to act now.
item.dc:creator: Maia Spoto and Jill Cowan
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran for The New York Times
item.media:description: Dario Amodei of Anthropic called for slowing the A.I. development in a 3,800-word essay over the weekend.

item.title: Russian Businessman With Putin Ties Paid for Donald Trump Jr.’s Wedding Party
item.description: The payments, totaling hundreds of thousands of dollars, represented an extraordinary flouting of ethical norms for an American president’s family member.
item.dc:creator: Ben Protess
item.media:credit: Alex Kent/The New York Times; Yulia Morozova/Reuters
item.media:description: The president’s eldest son, Donald Trump Jr., accepted the gifts from Umar Kremlev, the president of the International Boxing Association, according to people with knowledge of the matter.

item.title: Architects of Japan’s Easy-Money Policies Are Changing Their Minds
item.description: As the Bank of Japan weighs another rate increase on Friday, a divide over how Japan should confront inflation is widening.
item.dc:creator: River Akira Davis and Hisako Ueno
item.media:credit: Andrew Caballero-Reynolds/Agence France-Presse — Getty Images
item.media:description: A wholesale market in Tokyo. For most of the past four years, inflation has remained above the Bank of Japan’s 2 percent target.

item.title: ‘Widow’s Bay’ Dominates, and 7 Other Takeaways From the 2026 Emmys
item.description: The Apple TV horror-comedy about a haunted island took home 14 Emmys, including the awards for best comedy, lead actor, writing, directing and supporting actor and actress.
item.dc:creator: John Koblin
item.media:credit: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters
item.media:description: Katie Dippold and the cast and crew of “Widow’s Bay” accepting the Emmy Award for Outstanding Comedy Series on Monday night.

item.title: Have Thoughts on the Emmy’s Red Carpet? Join Our Readers in the Comments.
item.description: Television’s biggest stars have walked the carpet. Now that you’ve seen what everyone is wearing and voted for your favorite looks, we invite you to comment on a few of the styles.
item.dc:creator: The Styles Desk

item.title: Emmy Winners 2026: See the Full List
item.description: Here are the winners from the 78th Emmy Awards.
item.dc:creator: Shivani Gonzalez
item.media:credit: Mario Anzuoni/Reuters
item.media:description: Katie Dippold accepted the best comedy Emmy on Monday night for her hit Apple TV show “Widow’s Bay,” which won 14 statuettes this year, more than any other series.

item.title: Mitch McConnell Returns to Senate After Three Month Absence
item.description: Senator Mitch McConnell, the 84-year-old Kentucky Republican and former leader, had been absent for more than 13 weeks after a health incident, fueling questions about his ability to continue serving.
item.dc:creator: Catie Edmondson, Carl Hulse and Michael Gold
item.media:credit: Tierney L. Cross for The New York Times
item.media:description: Senator Mitch McConnell arriving for a vote at the Capitol on Monday afternoon. He had not been seen there since he last cast a floor vote on June 11.

item.title: N.Y. Democratic House Candidate Admits to Bondage Photo Shoot
item.description: Christopher Gallant, who is running against Representative Nick LaLota on Long Island, acknowledged that the photos that surfaced in media reports on Monday were legitimate.
item.dc:creator: Andy Newman
item.media:credit: Patrick McMullan, via Getty Images
item.media:description: Christopher Gallant said he was “not embarrassed or ashamed” of the photos, which were taken around 2010 for a company called Mr. S Leather.

item.title: Gavin Newsom Says He Won’t Run in 2028 if Kamala Harris Does
item.description: The comments made to CNN, if taken at face value, seemed to fly in the face of the California governor’s presidential ambitions.
item.dc:creator: Reid J. Epstein
item.media:credit: Karsten Moran and Nick Hagen for The New York Times
item.media:description: Gov. Gavin Newsom of California and former Vice President Kamala Harris are widely seen as potential 2028 presidential candidates.

item.title: Whistle-Blower: Federal Agents May Have Broken State Laws in Search For Voter Fraud
item.description: Agents expressed concern about being directed by top Homeland Security leaders to use private information to look up voter records in state databases.
item.dc:creator: Nick Corasaniti and Hamed Aleaziz
item.media:credit: Matt Gade/Associated Press
item.media:description: New citizens registered to vote following a naturalization ceremony at Mount Rushmore in South Dakota last year.

item.title: An Heir to a Thai Beer Empire Accused His Brother of Sexual Abuse. Then He Took on His Family.
item.description: Siranudh Scott, an heir to Thailand’s Singha beer empire, has prompted a rare public reckoning about a topic considered taboo.
item.dc:creator: Sui-Lee Wee
item.media:credit: Lauren DeCicca for The New York Times
item.media:description: Siranudh Scott at home in Bangkok.

item.title: Immigrants’ Lawyers Say U.S. Is Redacting Documents Proving Legal Status
item.description: Many noncitizens need immigration records the government has to prove their legal stay and resist deportation. The government is redacting and withholding those documents, lawyers say.
item.dc:creator: Minho Kim
item.media:credit: Alan Nakkash for The New York Times
item.media:description: Federal law mandates that agencies provide immigrants facing deportations needed documents “pertaining to the alien’s admission or presence.”

item.title: Key West Feels the Pain of Trump Decision on Haitians
item.description: The end of legal protections for Haitian immigrants nationally has jolted the labor market in this remote vacation destination in Florida where many live and work.
item.dc:creator: David Ovalle
item.media:credit: Mark Hedden for The New York Times
item.media:description: A Haitian immigrant who works at a supermarket in Key West leaves home less often since losing Temporary Protected Status in July.

item.title: Judge Blocks Trump Rule Aimed at International Students and Journalists
item.description: Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV wrote that the administration’s reasons for a rule limiting the length of stay for academics and journalists were “exceptionally weak.”
item.dc:creator: Chris Cameron
item.media:credit: Lucy Lu for The New York Times
item.media:description: A rally in support of international students at Harvard University last year. The Trump administration rule would have shortened the length of visas for international students, academics and foreign journalists.

item.title: Bob Mackie, Cher and the Ultimate Revenge Dress

item.dc:creator: Jacob Bernstein
item.media:credit: Bettmann, via Getty Images

item.title: Bob Mackie, Designer Who ‘Dressed Every Spangly Woman in Show Business,’ Dies at 87
item.description: His sequined gowns and outrageous costumes threw clouds of glitter at American fashion for over half a century.
item.dc:creator: Penelope Green
item.media:credit: Richard Drew/Associated Press
item.media:description: Bob Mackie in 2001. He designed beaded, rhinestoned, feathered and often winged creations that bedazzled and elevated celebrities like Carol Burnett, Cher, Diana Ross and RuPaul.

item.title: Bob Mackie: A Life in Pictures
item.description: The designer was known for his flashy, sparkly designs for Cher, Diana Ross, Tina Turner and countless others.
